Smile Party (Japan) — Grokipedia
In 2019, Akasaka achieved the party's most notable success by winning a seat in Tokyo's Minato Ward assembly after repeated unsuccessful runs in various elections.

The Smile Party was established in 2006 under the original name Japan Smile Party (日本スマイル党) by Mac Akasaka (real name Makoto Tonami), a businessman and chair of the Smile Therapy Association since 2004, to advance "Smile Therapy" as a political platform for improving mental health, promoting positivity, and pursuing social reforms.
In 2009, the party changed its name from Japan Smile Party (日本スマイル党, Nihon Sumairu-tō) to Smile Party (スマイル党, Sumairu-tō).
The renaming occurred shortly before the August 2009 general election for the House of Representatives, in which the party fielded candidates, including in Tokyo's 1st district.

Since Mac Akasaka secured the Smile Party's first elected position in the April 2019 Minato Ward Assembly election, garnering 1,144 votes to win a seat after multiple prior unsuccessful campaigns, the party has maintained a limited presence in Tokyo local politics.
Tokyo electoral district

The party has not gained additional seats or achieved significant electoral breakthroughs since 2019, with Akasaka's council term ending in 2023 and no further assembly representation; its activities remain centered on Tokyo and its core platform of smile therapy and social reforms. The official website continues to promote its longstanding policies without major new announcements.

Broader goals tied to mental health include raising Japan's Gross National Happiness (GNH) index through policy measures, the creation of a Basic Law on Happiness Measures, and the establishment of a Ministry of Happiness. The party positions these initiatives as supporting societal positivity and the mental well-being of vulnerable groups, including those with mental disabilities.

The Smile Party has participated in elections for Japan's national legislature, the Diet, by fielding candidates primarily in Tokyo constituencies for both the House of Representatives and the House of Councillors, though it has never secured a seat in either chamber.
in 2007 (initially under the Japan Smile Party name), 2010, and 2013, employing tactics such as dancing atop vehicles to 1980s music in busy areas like Shibuya to attract attention.
For House of Representatives elections, the party nominated Mac Akasaka in Tokyo's 1st district in 2009.

More recently, the party has endorsed or fielded candidates in national contests, including a recommendation for an independent in Tokyo's 7th district in the 2021 House of Representatives election and a candidate in the Tokyo electoral district for the 2022 House of Councillors election.
Tokyo gubernatorial elections

The Smile Party has participated in several Tokyo gubernatorial elections by fielding its leader Mac Akasaka as its candidate in multiple races, using these high-profile contests to promote smile therapy, mental positivity, and related social reforms through distinctive and flamboyant campaigns.
Akasaka ran under the Smile Party banner in the Tokyo gubernatorial elections of 2007, 2011, December 16, 2012 (receiving 38,855 votes)

Akasaka did not run in the subsequent 2020 or 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial elections. In 2020, the Smile Party fielded a different candidate, Hiroshi Komiyama, who received 10,935 votes. No candidate was fielded by the party in 2024. In later years, Akasaka indicated he would no longer run for governor.
The Smile Party has participated in a limited number of gubernatorial and mayoral elections outside Tokyo, primarily through the candidacy of its leader Mac Akasaka.

In the 2011 Osaka Prefecture gubernatorial election, Akasaka ran as the Smile Party candidate. His campaign featured a distinctive policy broadcast in which he appeared in aerobics attire, spoke in Kansai dialect, and performed a routine ending with "Smilebics" exercises. He received 21,479 votes (0.59% of the total), placing seventh among seven candidates.

These candidacies highlighted the party's emphasis on flamboyant, attention-seeking campaigns but yielded no victories and consistently low vote shares. No other gubernatorial or mayoral elections outside Tokyo are documented for the party.

The Smile Party has participated in local assembly elections primarily in Tokyo's special wards, often with leader Mac Akasaka as the candidate. These efforts have generally resulted in low vote shares consistent with the party's minor status, but they have contributed to its visibility through eccentric campaigning.

The Smile Party's most significant electoral achievement came in the April 2019 Minato Ward assembly election in Tokyo, where leader Mac Akasaka won a seat with 1,144 votes, placing 30th among 54 candidates competing for 34 seats.
This marked the party's first victory after Akasaka's 14th candidacy across various elections, including multiple bids for Tokyo governor and national office.
In Tokyo gubernatorial elections, the party has consistently fielded candidates but received modest support; for example, Akasaka garnered 15,070 votes in the 2014 contest.

Following his 2019 election to the Minato Ward Assembly in Tokyo, Akasaka established a one-person "Smile Party" faction within the assembly, further illustrating the party's leadership structure as tied closely to his individual role.

The Japanese Smile That Puzzles the World
[Kotoba – The Way of Japanese] –
Missionary Francis Xavier, who arrived in Japan in 1549, described the Japanese as people who valued honor and bravery.
Engelbert Kaempfer, a physician attached to the Dutch trading post during the Edo period, depicted the Japanese as polite, clean, and diligent.
Furthermore, Rutherford Alcock, a British diplomat who came to Japan at the end of the Edo period, wrote that the Japanese were "gentle, polite, amiable, and smiling people."
Tracing the records of foreigners, we can see that in addition to politeness and diligence, a cheerful demeanor was also commonly found in the Japanese.
So, what exactly is this Japanese "cheerfulness" or "smile"?

The Japanese Smile That Puzzles the World
[Kotoba – The Way of Japanese] –
Missionary Francis Xavier, who arrived in Japan in 1549, described the Japanese as people who valued honor and bravery.
Engelbert Kaempfer, a physician attached to the Dutch trading post during the Edo period, depicted the Japanese as polite, clean, and diligent.
Furthermore, Rutherford Alcock, a British diplomat who came to Japan at the end of the Edo period, wrote that the Japanese were "gentle, polite, amiable, and smiling people."
Tracing the records of foreigners, we can see that in addition to politeness and diligence, a cheerful demeanor was also commonly found in the Japanese.
So, what exactly is this Japanese "cheerfulness" or "smile"?

“No Bad Emotions: How to Truly Smile”

This talk was given to promote mental health in the Philippines, but regardless of nationality, it may also resonate with those who feel they must “be proper” or “always be positive,” and as a result,
end up suppressing or denying their own emotions.
